summary:
IGNIS is an SI-powered dashboard and agent harness for NASA’s microgravity combustion data. It reads all 19 ISS combustion investigations in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics system (41,004 files, 856 runs), classifies and ranks them for the air a crew will breathe (spacecraft, Moon base at 30% oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less, spacesuit) and answers questions in plain language with the source behind every number.

Its core is forecasting. Instead of training black-box networks, a frontier SI writes each model weight by weight from physics, NASA papers and data (weight-space programming), so every weight carries a written reason and a wrong forecast is fixed by rewriting one number. Scored on held-out NASA tests, these written models beat textbook laws, trained networks and seven published peer-reviewed models. A fabric-fire model written from 2 cm strips burned on the ISS forecast NASA’s 40 cm Saffire fires 4.3 times more accurately than the baseline, without changing a single weight.

For NASA this supports prevention, detection and suppression decisions for Artemis habitats: forecasts for the fires NASA cannot afford to light.
details:
What it does

IGNIS is an SI-powered dashboard and agent harness over all 19 ISS combustion investigations in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics system: 41,004 files and 856 runs of droplets, flames, burning fabrics and plastics, and smoke. You ask in plain language, and IGNIS does three things:

  • Finds the experiments that answer your question, with the NASA source behind every number.
  • Ranks them for the air a crew will breathe (ISS, Moon base at 30% oxygen or more, spacesuit) and for fire prevention, detection and suppression.
  • Forecasts whether a fire keeps burning, how fast, and when it goes out, with an uncertainty range.

How it’s creative

The forecasting models are written, not trained. Using weight-space programming (MIT CSAIL, November 2026), a frontier SI reads the physics, NASA’s papers and the data, and writes every weight of a small neural network itself, each with its reason. The result is a glass box: every forecast can be explained, and a mistake is fixed by editing one number, not by retraining. Because the models follow physics rather than memorising data, they carry over to conditions they never saw.

Results on NASA data the models never saw

  • Beyond its data: a fire model written from 2 cm strips burned on the Space Station forecast NASA’s 40 cm Saffire spacecraft fires 4.3× better than the baseline, with no weight changed.
    • GPT-6 Luna rises from 43 to 77. That matches OpenAI’s flagship GPT-6 Astra at 1/7 of the cost: 108 answers per dollar against 15.
    • GPT-6.1 Terra inside IGNIS outscores the flagship (80 vs 77) for about 30% less.
    • Inside IGNIS, every model is right 94–100% of the times it answers.
  • It reads closely: the agent found 13 errors in NASA’s public tables.

Impact

The Artemis Moon base will breathe 30% oxygen or more, where materials burn more readily, and NASA can’t light every fire it will face. IGNIS turns 19 investigations of past experiments into ranked evidence and checked forecasts for crew safety. It works with any SI and makes a cheap model perform like a flagship, so this analysis is affordable at scale. When NASA flies a new experiment, the same harness writes the next model. In short: forecasts for the fires NASA can’t afford to light.

Built with

Rust (Axum, Tokio), React with TypeScript and Vite, Codex App Server with MCP tools, and Cloudflare. The SI models are Claude (Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5) and OpenAI GPT-6 and GPT-6.1.
